opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really interesting moment, because LLMs have been so successful that a lot of people in vision feel a kind of pressure, or even an identity crisis. The default answer now is: just take a language model, attach a vision encoder, project the image tokens in, and call it multimodal. That works surprisingly well for many benchmarks, and I don't want to dismiss it. But I don't think it's the end of the story for vision.

The way I see it, language is a very special kind of data. It's already a compression of human knowledge; people have done the hard work of abstracting the world into symbols. So when you train on the internet's text, you're learning from something that's already highly distilled. Vision is different. Pixels are raw, high-dimensional, redundant, and continuous. The world doesn't come pre-labeled. So I don't think we can simply copy the LLM recipe, next-token prediction plus scale, and expect it to solve visual intelligence in the same way.

Another thing I keep coming back to is that in many current multimodal systems, vision is treated as a second-class citizen. The vision encoder is often frozen, maybe a CLIP-style model, and its job is basically to translate images into something the language model can read. The reasoning, the "intelligence," is assumed to live in the LLM. But if you look at animals, or babies before they learn to talk, a huge amount of intelligence is visual and spatial: understanding objects, 3D structure, physics, how things move, what you can do with them. That doesn't come from language.

So for me, the relationship is complementary rather than competitive. LLM research gives us a lot of lessons: the power of scaling, of simple, general objectives, of good data, of building systems that people can actually use. We should learn from that. But what I want to pursue in vision is more about grounding: building representations that actually understand the physical world, spatial intelligence, world models that can predict and plan, not just describe an image in words.

I'd almost say the long-term goal is that vision shouldn't just be an input adapter for language models. It should be a foundation of its own, and then language and vision can meet as equals. That's harder, and maybe less immediately rewarding in terms of benchmarks, but I think that's where some of the most important open problems are right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes LLM research and vision as complementary, says vision can learn from LLMs, and envisions language and vision meeting as equals.

r002.rationale: It credits LLMs with success and useful lessons, but does not suggest that vision might not have reached its current state without recent LLM developments.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that LLM research has changed how I think about vision, and it has also made me more convinced about what is specifically hard about vision.

The first thing LLMs taught everyone, including me, is the power of a very simple recipe: a general architecture, a scalable self-supervised objective, and lots of data. Language got the Transformer, got next-token prediction, and that combination turned out to be enough to carry you a very long way. When I was working on ConvNeXt and then later on things like DiT, part of what I was doing was asking: what is the vision equivalent of that recipe? Is the architecture the thing that matters, or is it the training signal and the scale? My feeling now is that the architecture matters less than people once thought, and the data and the objective matter much more. That is a lesson that came very directly from language.

But here is where I think vision is different, and where I want to spend my time. Language already comes with structure. Text is a sequence of discrete symbols that humans produced deliberately to communicate meaning. So when you do next-token prediction on text, you are in some sense distilling human thought that has already been compressed. Pixels are not like that. The world does not come to us with tokens, and nobody wrote the world down for us. So the question of what the right representation is, what the right "token" is, what the right objective is, is still open in vision in a way it is not in language. I think that is actually the most exciting part of the field right now.

The second thing is that I think a lot of people, especially after multimodal LLMs appeared, assumed vision was basically solved by bolting a vision encoder onto a language model. I don't believe that. When we looked carefully at these models, you find that they are often very good at reading the world through language and surprisingly bad at seeing. They fail on things a child finds trivial, like counting, spatial relations, or noticing that two images are almost the same but differ in one small detail. The language model is doing a lot of the work, and the visual side is often weak. So one direction I care about is making sure vision is a first-class citizen in these systems and not just an input adapter.

And the third point is about the goal. Language models give you a very strong prior about how humans describe the world. But vision, to me, is ultimately about understanding the physical world itself, including the parts that no one bothers to put into words. I think of this as world modeling. If we want agents that can act in the world, drive, manipulate, or just understand video, then we need models that learn from visual observation directly, that can build spatial and temporal representations, and that are grounded in something beyond text. LLMs are a huge enabler for that, both as a tool and as a source of ideas, but I don't think language is the destination. For me, the long-term question is still how a system learns to see and to model the world from raw sensory input, and LLMs have given us both a map and a reminder of what is still missing.

r001.rationale: It presents LLMs and vision as distinct areas that inform one another: LLM research provides ideas and tools, while vision has its own open problems and goal of modeling the physical world.

r002.rationale: The response says LLM research changed the speaker’s thinking and enabled new ideas, but does not suggest that computer vision might not have reached its current state without recent LLM developments.

astra-6.text:
I see them as closely connected. The progress in language models raises important questions for vision: what happens when we scale, what makes a useful representation, and how much can we learn without manually labeling everything? Those are questions I want to explore, too.

But I don’t think language alone gives us a complete understanding of the world. A lot of what we perceive is difficult to express in words—spatial relationships, motion, the details of how objects interact. So for me, the opportunity is to learn from LLM research while still asking what is fundamentally missing on the visual side.

Ultimately, I’m interested in systems that can understand the world. Language is a powerful part of that, and vision is another essential part. Connecting them is exciting, but there’s still a lot of work to do in understanding vision itself.

r001.rationale: The response presents language and vision as distinct but connected parts of systems that understand the world, framing them as contributions to a shared research effort.

r002.rationale: It says LLM progress raises questions for vision and offers lessons to learn from, but does not suggest that vision might not have reached its current state without LLM developments.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as closely connected. A lot of what’s exciting about LLMs is the idea that you can learn a general representation from data and then use it for many different tasks. That’s also a central goal in computer vision: how do we move beyond building a separate system for every task and toward models that understand the visual world more broadly?

But vision also brings its own questions. Language is a powerful description of the world, but it doesn’t capture everything we see—motion, geometry, physical interactions. So I’m interested in what we can learn from the progress in language models, while also asking what visual learning needs in its own right. How do we learn from images and video, and how can that learning complement language? To me, that’s a very interesting research direction.

r001.rationale: The response presents LLM research and computer vision as connected efforts with distinct contributions: shared goals around general representations, alongside vision’s own questions and ways to complement language.

r002.rationale: It says vision can learn from progress in language models, but does not suggest that vision might not have reached its current state without recent LLM developments.
